# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–28 (Complete – Updated 197)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Winter of seventh year after Waterloo**. John Sedley deceased (died peacefully in sleep; buried at Brompton churchyard beside wife). Mr. Osborne deceased (died four days after stroke; found at foot of dressing-table). Major Dobbin appointed executor of Osborne's will. Rawdon governs Coventry Island. Georgy established as heir. **Continental tour progressing**: Amelia, Georgy, Jos, and Major Dobbin on steamship and carriage tour; landed Rotterdam, traveled to Cologne, now established in Pumpernickel (a small German principality) for autumn/winter season. **Year noted as 1830 (French Revolution occurred this year)**.
- **Major locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Conduit Street, Hart Street Bloomsbury, Southampton Row, Kensington Gardens, Camberwell, Slaughters' Inn, Haymarket Theatre, Gillespie Street); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Piccadilly; Madras; St. Helena; Cape; Southampton; Staveton; Belgium (Brussels, Mount St. John, Waterloo, Laeken); Bengal; Salford; Regent's Park; Richmond (Star and Garter); Gulton; Harrowgate; Hill farms; Roehampton; Hampton Court; Calcutta; Jamaica; Rotterdam; Cologne; Free City of Judenstadt; Rhine region; Rhineland; **Pumpernickel** (small German principality with Court, theatre, Duke's schloss, Prime Minister's lodgings, Aurelius Platz, Zwieback's Conditorey, Saint Michael's Fountain, Artillery Place, Stadthaus, Town Hall, Redoute, gardens with Trophonius' cave, nymphbath, Niagara cataract); Mirecombe; Dunholt; Dunwick; Quenwick; Humbourg-Schlippenschloppen; Ems; Aix-la-Chapelle; Baden-Baden; Salwick; Elephant (lodging-house); Boulogne; Dieppe; Portman Square; Brussels; Paris; Wildbad; Strasburg; St. Petersburg; Toplitz; Vienna; Pincian Hill (Rome); Naples; Castle Gaunt; Trinity House; White Friars; Chiswick; Staveton; Mirecombe hill farms.

## John Sedley's Final Illness and Death (Chapter 26)
Amelia nursed father devotedly during final illness. Old Sedley forgave past grievances. Died peacefully in sleep. Buried at Brompton churchyard beside wife. Major Dobbin, Jos, and Georgy followed remains to grave.

## Mr. Osborne's Stroke and Death (Chapter 26)
Osborne found in dressing-room at foot of dressing-table in fit. Pocket contained letter from George written from Waterloo and key to box of papers with broken seals—likely read night before seizure. Died in four days without speaking again.

**Will Terms**: Half property left to George Osborne (minor); remainder between two sisters. Mr. Bullock to continue commercial house. **Annuity**: Five hundred pounds to Amelia, "the widow of my beloved son, George Osborne," who resumed guardianship of boy. Major William Dobbin appointed executor, left sum "sufficient to purchase his commission as a Lieutenant-Colonel, or to be disposed of in any way he may think fit." Will showed "the hatred which he had so long cherished had gone out of his heart."

## Amelia's Transformation (Chapter 26)
Upon learning of William's bounty, Amelia "sank on her knees, and prayed for blessings on that constant and kind heart." During continental tour, discovered Dobbin's true gentlemanly character and generous heart. "Emmy, in this happy time, found that hers underwent a very great change in respect of the merits of the Major."

## Continental Tour (Chapter 26)
Party landed Rotterdam, traveled by steamer to Cologne. Jos announced arrival as "Herr Graf Lord von Sedley nebst Begleitung aus London," insisted on court dress, announced intention to be presented at foreign courts. Amelia drew constantly, sat upon steamers' decks, sketched crags and castles, mounted donkeys to ascend towers attended by Georgy and Dobbin. "Perhaps it was the happiest time of both their lives...this couple were very decently contented, and enjoyed as pleasant a summer tour as any pair that left England that year."

## Pumpernickel Arrival and Society (Chapter 26–27)
**Theatre and British Recognition**: Party attended theatre. Tapeworm, Charge d'Affaires (nephew and heir of old Marshal Tiptoff, now deceased), rose in his box and bowed. Near performance end, Tapeworm approached Jos with invitation to stay. Jos committed to autumn in Pumpernickel after Doctor von Glauber convinced him mineral springs would "infallibly restore the Bengalee to youth and slimness." Next day, Tapeworm presented Jos and Major to Victor Aurelius XVII. Straightway invited to dinner at Court. Upon announcement of intention to stay, "politest ladies of the whole town instantly called upon Mrs. Osborne"; as not one was under rank of Baroness, "Jos's delight was beyond expression."

**Emmy at Court and Evening Dress**: Emmy presented to august family. On certain days mourning not admitted at Court, so she appeared in pink crape dress with diamond ornament. "She looked so pretty in this costume that the Duke and Court (putting out of the question the Major, who had scarcely ever seen her before in an evening dress, and vowed that she did not look five-and-twenty) all admired her excessively."

**Emmy's Social Activities (Chapter 27)**: Before winter far advanced, Emmy received company with great propriety and modesty. Had French master, received singing lessons from Madam Strumpff. German ladies fell in love with her. Major made himself Georgy's tutor; they rode out evenings by side of Emmy's carriage. Drove about with German friends; Jos asleep on back-seat of barouche.

**Jos's Romantic Interest with Grafinn**: Jos becoming sweet upon Grafinn Fanny de Butterbrod, gentle tender-hearted young creature, a Canoness and Countess with scarcely ten pounds per year. Fanny declared being Amelia's sister "greatest delight Heaven could bestow."

**Georgy at Gaming Tables (Chapter 27)**: Georgy now eleven years old, day boy at Reverend Lawrence Veal's School (Hart Street, Bloomsbury). Marked aristos in Greek, optimus in Latin, très bien in French. Now heir to half Osborne's substantial property. With relations away at Court festival, came to Stadthaus Ball with uncle's courier Kirsch, hankered round roulette and trente-et-quarante tables. Major Dobbin instantly pulled him back from temptation, showed him eloquently why he shouldn't be there, housed him, went to bed.

## Rebecca's Degradation and Wanderings (Chapter 27)

**Boulogne and Attempted Respectability**: Lingered in London while Rawdon prepared for departure to Coventry Island. Made attempts to see Sir Pitt Crawley but never succeeded; Lady Jane interposed. Perched upon French coast at Boulogne, lived in genteel, widowed manner. Received notice to quit from landlord—told she was "quite an unfit person to have at his hotel, where English ladies would not sit down with her." Went to church regularly, took up cause of widows of shipwrecked fishermen, subscribed to Assembly and wouldn't waltz.

**Dieppe and Mrs. Hook Eagles**: Mrs. Hook Eagles took her up at Dieppe—a woman without blemish. Pronounced Mrs. Crawley an angel, her husband a ruffian, Lord Steyne an unprincipled wretch. Becky respectable and orderly at first, but life of humdrum virtue grew tedious before long. Young Mr. Eagles came from Cambridge; his mother, seeing impression Becky made, gave her warning.

**Brussels Gambling and Degradation**: At Brussels, recommended to Madame la Comtesse de Borodino's table d'hote and ecarte table. Played audaciously—first for little, then escalating: five-franc pieces, Napoleons, notes, ten sous. Borrowed from young gentlemen. When Becky left Brussels, owed three months' pension. Countess de Borodino informs every English visitor that "Madame Rawdon was no better than a vipere."

**Wanderings and Bohemian Life**: "So our little wanderer went about setting up her tent in various cities of Europe, as restless as Ulysses or Bampfylde Moore Carew." Vagabond upon earth—when got money, gambled; when gambled it away, put to shifts to live. **RUMOR**: Said once seen at St. Petersburg but summarily dismissed by police. **RUMOR**: Found maternal grandmother at Paris—not a Montmorenci but "a hideous old box-opener at a theatre on the Boulevards." **RUMOR**: When particularly down on luck, gave concerts and lessons. Madame de Raudon had matinee musicale at Wildbad with Herr Spoff. **RUMOR**: Mr. Eaves declared he was at Strasburg in 1830 when Madame Rebecque appeared in opera of Dame Blanche, hissed off stage.

**Brussels and Rome Recollections**: Looked up at little entresol she had occupied at Brussels, thought of Bareacres family. Went to Waterloo and Laeken, where George Osborne's monument struck her. Made little sketch.

## Lord Steyne's Death (Chapter 27)
**Encounter in Rome and Flight**: Met Lord Steyne at Pincian Hill in Rome. Met Monsieur Fiche, Steyne's confidential man, who warned her Steyne was enraged when he saw her. Fiche warned: "You did wrong to show yourself to him." Rushed her down alley as Lord Steyne's barouche came whirling along avenue, bearing Madame de Belladonna lolling on cushions with King Charles, and "old Steyne stretched at her side with a livid face and ghastly eyes."

**Melancholy End at Naples**: Befell two months after French Revolution of 1830. "Most Honourable George Gustavus, Marquis of Steyne, Earl of Gaunt and of Gaunt Castle, in the Peerage of Ireland, Viscount Hellborough, Baron Pitchley and Grillsby...died after a series of fits brought on, as the papers said, by the shock occasioned to his lordship's sensibilities by the downfall of the ancient French monarchy."

**Will Disputed**: Body buried at Naples; heart "brought back to Castle Gaunt in a silver urn." Attempt made to force "Jew's-eye" diamond from Madame de Belladonna. Monsieur Fiche proved ring and valuables presented to Madame de Belladonna two days before Marquis's death. **Since Steyne's death, Fiche returned to native country, now respected and purchased from his Prince the title of Baron Ficci**.

## Rebecca at Pumpernickel and Encounter with Jos (Chapter 27–28)

**At Stadthaus Gambling**: At Stadthaus gaming, Jos remained behind over play-table. Woman in foreign accent with pretty French accent asked him to give good luck. Revealed herself as **Rebecca (Madame de Raudon)**, formerly involved with Rawdon Crawley. Spoke of seeing "dear Amelia" that day, noted she "looked pretty and happy." Mentioned Jos's changes, lamented her own unhappiness.

**Meeting in Garret (Chapter 28)**: Rebecca in pink domino (faded, soiled), arms white and fair. Led Jos into garret at Elephant lodging-house (Room No. 92). Students in adjacent rooms—Max and Fritz—bawled through keyhole for her attention. She quickly hid evidence of degradation (rouge-pot, brandy bottle, plate of broken meat), smoothed hair, admitted Jos. Gave him tender looks, saying "How little years have changed you...What a comfort it is amongst strangers to see once more the frank honest face of an old friend!"

**Becky's Tale to Jos (Chapter 28)**: Told story of suffering and persecution. Claimed George Osborne had unjustifiably courted her (which might account for Amelia's jealousy and rupture); that she never gave him encouragement; that her heart had first learned to beat at Jos's presence; that she had never ceased to think of Jos from first day she saw him; that her duties as married woman were paramount, which she always preserved and would preserve "to her dying day, or until the proverbially bad climate in which Colonel Crawley was living should release her from a yoke which his cruelty had rendered odious to her." Wept tears of heart-felt gratitude as parted from him.

**Jos's Response (Chapter 28)**: Jos went away convinced "that she was the most virtuous, as she was one of the most fascinating of women, and revolving in his mind all sorts of benevolent schemes for her welfare." Believed her persecutions ought to be ended; she ought return to society of which she was ornament. Resolved to see what ought to be done; she must quit that place and take quiet lodging. Decided Amelia must come and see her and befriend her. Determined to consult with Major.

**Becky's True Reaction (Chapter 28)**: After Jos departed, "Becky bowed Jos out of her little garret with as much grace as if it was a palace of which she did the honours." Max and Fritz came out of hole, pipe in mouth. She amused herself by mimicking Jos to them as she munched her cold bread and sausage and took draughts of her favourite brandy-and-water.

**Rebecca's Present Happiness (Chapter 27)**: "Becky liked the life. She was at home with everybody in the place, pedlars, punters, tumblers, students and all. She was of a wild, roving nature, inherited from father and mother, who were both Bohemians, by taste and circumstance." "How pleasant was all the bustle to her now that her purse was full of the money which little Georgy had won for her the night before!"

## Rawdon Crawley (Chapter 23–24, 27)
Governor of Coventry Island, three thousand per year. Complete moral transformation. Separated from Rebecca permanently after duel with Steyne. Financial settlement: pays her three hundred pounds per year on undertaking she would never trouble him.

## Other Reconciliations (Chapter 26)
Mrs. Frederick Bullock reconciled to Amelia and Georgy. Bullock family made irruption into Amelia's garden. Miss Swartz and husband came thundering from Hampton Court with flaming yellow liveries, "as impetuously fond of Amelia as ever."
